I think the basic thing that we're confusing is "news" with "information" or "intelligence". News articles are by definition not a good source of information for making policy decisions because the plural of anecdote isn't data. If we want objective information on things like immigration, war, and economics we need to be looking at very dry subject specific reports and studies. (Unfortunately, these are things we'll never likely get a chance to look at, because they exist either behind walls as confidential or classified for the benefit of the people that paid for them to be conducted.)

Think about the last time you worked in an industry and were privy to confidential documents, now think about how the public media treats that subject matter. Why would we then turn the page and expect them to treat a different subject any differently.

I have worked in the media in mid 90's and for 4 very bad years .

News can be a source of information but objectivity lies entirely on the audience (us) and our ability to cross check , analyze and draw conclusions while remaining skeptical . The idea that someone can read a single site or a newspaper and safely call him/herself informed have died long ago .
